key_points.base: I'd start with the decision the model supports: who gets a retention offer, and what an offer costs
points: I'd start with the decision the model supports: who gets a retention offer, and what an offer costs versus a lost customer.
Then I'd define churn and the prediction window, build features only from data available at prediction time, split by time, and baseline with logistic regression.
Churn is imbalanced, so accuracy is meaningless.
I'd use precision and recall at the top-k the team can actually act on, plus calibration.
XGBoost is justified if it beats the baseline by enough to matter, and SHAP explains it.
Production-ready means the false-positive cost is acceptable, not that a metric crossed a number.

key_points.base: I'd separate data drift (inputs shift, measured with PSI or KS on key features) from model drift (pe
points: I'd separate data drift (inputs shift, measured with PSI or KS on key features) from model drift (performance degrades, which needs labels that often arrive late).
Input and prediction distributions are the leading signal, and real performance follows when labels land.
The valuable part is the action policy: thresholds tied to impact, and a clear rule for when drift means investigate, retrain, or roll back.
To avoid alert fatigue I'd alert on a few high-importance features and an aggregate score, not every column.

key_points.base: History only shows what happened under past budgets. I'd model the demand drivers (revenue plan, att
points: History only shows what happened under past budgets.
I'd model the demand drivers (revenue plan, attrition, ramp time, open requisitions) and treat approved budget as a constraint on supply.
I'd compare a seasonal baseline, a regression with drivers, and ARIMA using rolling-origin backtests.
If the model says 150 and Finance budgeted 80, I wouldn't defend or discard the number.
I'd show the gap, the assumptions driving it, and scenarios.
A hiring pause is a regime shift, so I'd flag those months instead of learning from them as normal.

key_points.base: Every feature is computed as of a cutoff date using only data available then, via as-of joins or a p
points: Every feature is computed as of a cutoff date using only data available then, via as-of joins or a point-in-time feature store.
I'd verify by recomputing features at past cutoffs.
'Days since last payment' leaks if it's calculated from the full table.
From 10,000 candidates I'd prune by domain priors, stability across time, and importance under time-based validation, not on a single fold.
For credit score missing on 40% of customers, I'd keep missingness as a signal, impute inside a pipeline fit only on training data, and check whether missingness correlates with the target.

key_points.base: First rule out a pipeline bug: schema, null rates, feature computation, and train/serve skew. Then c
points: First rule out a pipeline bug: schema, null rates, feature computation, and train/serve skew.
Then compare feature and target distributions between 2023 and 2024 and slice performance by segment and month to see where it broke.
If the world changed, as with the rate spike, it's covariate or concept shift.
Retraining helps only if the new regime is represented in the data.
Otherwise I'd add macro features, shorten the training window, or add a guardrail.
I'd decide with a time-based backtest, not a gut call.

key_points.base: I'd diagnose before acting. If training and validation error are both high and close, that's bias: u
points: I'd diagnose before acting.
If training and validation error are both high and close, that's bias: use a richer model, better features, or less regularization.
If training error is low and validation error is much higher, that's variance: more data, stronger regularization, simpler model, or bagging.
Learning curves show which regime I'm in, and more data mainly helps variance.
Regularization trades a little extra bias for a larger reduction in variance.

key_points.base: A model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate, so accuracy tells me nothing. I'd look at pr
points: A model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate, so accuracy tells me nothing.
I'd look at precision-recall curves and PR-AUC, because ROC-AUC can stay high when the number of negatives is huge.
The threshold comes from costs and capacity: missed fraud has a dollar cost, each false alert costs analyst time and customer friction, and the review team can only handle so many cases a day.
I'd also account for label delay by evaluating on mature cohorts, and remember that unlabeled fraud makes recall look better than it is.

key_points.base: Random folds mix future and past, so the model can learn patterns from after the test period and the
points: Random folds mix future and past, so the model can learn patterns from after the test period and the score is too optimistic.
I'd use walk-forward validation: train on data up to a cutoff, test on the next period, then move the cutoff forward.
If the label looks 30 days ahead, I'd leave a 30-day gap between train and test so labels don't overlap.
Expanding windows use all history and suit stable relationships, while sliding windows adapt faster when behavior drifts.
Hyperparameter tuning goes inside the training period with the same time-aware splits.

key_points.base: Not automatically. First I'd check the difference is real with a confidence interval from bootstrapp
points: Not automatically.

First I'd check the difference is real with a confidence interval from bootstrapping or repeated time-based folds, and translate it into the business metric (for example, extra customers retained per month) to see whether it covers the costs.
Then the non-metric factors: whether decisions must be explained, latency limits, how fragile the model is to drift, and the ongoing monitoring and retraining burden.
If the gain is small, I'd ship logistic regression, or ship the complex model only with SHAP-based explanations and monitoring in place.

key_points.base: I'd start by understanding why values are missing. If missingness is random, simple imputation is fi
points: I'd start by understanding why values are missing.
If missingness is random, simple imputation is fine.
If it depends on the value itself, such as high earners skipping an income field, mean imputation biases the data, and I'd add a missing-indicator feature.
Imputation goes inside the pipeline, fitted on training data only, to avoid leakage.
Tree-based models like XGBoost can handle missing values natively.
Real ones carry information, so I'd keep them and use robust methods or transformations like log, and only remove confirmed errors.

key_points.base: That gap suggests the model has memorized training patterns that don't generalize, meaning high vari
points: That gap suggests the model has memorized training patterns that don't generalize, meaning high variance.
Before changing the model I'd confirm the split is valid: no duplicates across sets, similar distributions, no leakage.
Then I'd plot learning curves: if validation error keeps falling with more data, collecting more helps; if it plateaus, reduce complexity.
I'd try, roughly in this order: a simpler model or stronger regularization, early stopping, feature pruning, more or augmented data, and cross-validation for a steadier estimate.
Each change is judged on the validation gap and the validation score together.

key_points.base: Bagging, as in a random forest, trains many deep, high-variance trees independently on bootstrap sam
points: Bagging, as in a random forest, trains many deep, high-variance trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them.
Averaging cancels much of the variance, so the individual trees can be deep.
Boosting builds trees sequentially, each fitting the errors of the ensemble so far, which reduces bias, so each tree can be shallow and weak; the learning rate scales how much each one contributes.
Boosting usually reaches higher accuracy on tabular data but is more sensitive to noisy labels and needs more tuning.
A random forest is a robust, low-tuning baseline that is hard to overfit badly.
I'd start with a forest and move to XGBoost when accuracy matters.

key_points.base: It depends on how the score is used. If we only rank cases and take the top K, AUC is what matters.
points: It depends on how the score is used.
If we only rank cases and take the top K, AUC is what matters.
If we use the output as a probability, for expected loss, pricing or cost-based thresholds, a score of 0.8 that really means 50% leads to wrong decisions.
I'd check with a reliability diagram and the Brier score, then recalibrate on a held-out set with Platt scaling or isotonic regression, which leaves AUC roughly unchanged.
Boosted trees and naive Bayes often need it; logistic regression is usually better behaved.
Calibration also drifts when class balance shifts, so I'd monitor it.

key_points.base: One-hot would create 50,000 sparse columns, slow training and overfit rare values. Options: frequenc
points: One-hot would create 50,000 sparse columns, slow training and overfit rare values.

Options: frequency or count encoding; target encoding computed out of fold with smoothing toward the global mean so rare categories can't memorize the label; learned embeddings for neural models; hashing; or grouping rare values into 'other' and using a coarser hierarchy such as region instead of zip.
CatBoost and LightGBM handle categories natively.
I'd always plan for unseen values at serving with a default bucket, and validate with a time-based split to check that the encoding isn't leaking.

key_points.base: For prediction, mostly no: a regularized linear model and a boosted model predict about as well. In
points: For prediction, mostly no: a regularized linear model and a boosted model predict about as well.

In a linear model the coefficients become unstable with large standard errors, so individual signs and sizes can't be trusted even though the combined effect is fine; ridge regularization or dropping one helps.
Trees use whichever feature gives the split first, so importance gets split or flips between runs.
For explanation, SHAP divides credit between them, so I'd report them as a group or remove one.
I drop a feature when interpretation, collection cost or stability matters, not as a reflex.

key_points.base: I'd turn it into expected value: flagging a customer costs the discount, and pays off only if the cu
points: I'd turn it into expected value: flagging a customer costs the discount, and pays off only if the customer would have churned and the discount saves them.

So I need the cost of the offer, the value of a saved customer and the discount's actual effect on churn, ideally from an experiment, since a high churn probability doesn't mean a customer is persuadable.
Then I sweep thresholds on held-out data using calibrated probabilities, choose the one that maximizes expected profit, and check capacity limits such as how many offers the team can send.
0.5 is arbitrary and F1 treats the two errors as equally costly.
I'd re-tune when base rates or costs shift.

key_points.base: Fanning residuals mean the error variance rises with the predicted value, known as heteroscedasticit
points: Fanning residuals mean the error variance rises with the predicted value, known as heteroscedasticity.
Point predictions can stay unbiased, but standard errors and confidence and prediction intervals are wrong, and large values may be fit worse in relative terms.

I'd plot residuals against fitted values and against each feature, then try modelling the log of the target (common for money), weighted least squares, robust standard errors, or a model that predicts spread too, such as quantile regression.
If only point accuracy matters it may be tolerable, but I'd check that the metric reflects relative error and not just absolute error.

key_points.base: Not yet. With 400 examples a single cross-validation estimate is very uncertain, so I'd report an in
points: With 400 examples a single cross-validation estimate is very uncertain, so I'd report an interval and use repeated or stratified CV.

Scores that high on small data usually point to a problem: duplicate or near-duplicate rows across folds, grouped data (the same patient or customer) split across folds, a feature that encodes the label, or hyperparameters tuned on the same folds.
I'd use grouped splits, nested CV for tuning and a final untouched holdout.
I'd also compare with a trivial baseline, read the confusion matrix, and ask whether real-world data resembles this sample.

key_points.base: ARIMA combines autoregression on past values (p), differencing to remove trend (d) and a moving aver
points: ARIMA combines autoregression on past values (p), differencing to remove trend (d) and a moving average of past errors (q).
Differencing aims at a stationary series, whose mean and variance don't drift, because the model's coefficients assume stable relationships.
I'd choose orders using autocorrelation plots and information criteria, then check them by walk-forward validation.
It works well for a single, short, regular series with few external drivers and is easy to explain.
It is a poor fit for many series at once, multiple seasonalities, holidays and rich external features, where boosted trees or other models do better.

key_points.base: Exponential smoothing is a quick, robust baseline for each series and needs little tuning. Prophet a
points: Exponential smoothing is a quick, robust baseline for each series and needs little tuning.
Prophet adds trend changes, seasonality and holidays with readable components, but it is not always the most accurate.
Gradient boosting trains one global model across all 200 products using lag features, calendar features, price and promotions, so it can learn from related products and handle short histories.

I'd compare all three with walk-forward validation on the metric the business cares about, ship the simple baseline first, and move to the global model if it wins by a margin that justifies the extra pipeline.

key_points.base: Separate models at each level won't sum. Bottom-up sums store forecasts, which is consistent but noi
points: Separate models at each level won't sum.
Bottom-up sums store forecasts, which is consistent but noisy for sparse stores.
Top-down splits a company forecast by historical proportions, which is smooth but loses store detail.

Reconciliation methods take forecasts from every level and adjust them jointly so they add up, weighting each by how reliable it is; this often improves accuracy at all levels because each level contributes information.
I would evaluate with walk-forward validation at every level, since the right choice depends on which level decisions are made at.

key_points.base: MAPE is easy to read but explodes when actuals are near zero and penalizes over-forecasts more than
points: MAPE is easy to read but explodes when actuals are near zero and penalizes over-forecasts more than under-forecasts, which can push models toward under-forecasting.
RMSE squares errors, so it punishes large misses and suits cases where a big miss is disproportionately costly.
WAPE divides total absolute error by total actuals, so it is stable and weights high-volume items more, which is often how the business thinks.
I would pick the metric from the cost of errors, report more than one, and evaluate at the level where decisions are made.

key_points.base: Matrix factorization learns a vector for each user and item from the interaction matrix so that thei
points: Matrix factorization learns a vector for each user and item from the interaction matrix so that their product predicts affinity; it captures taste patterns without needing item attributes, but it needs history and handles new items poorly.
A content-based approach scores items by similarity to what a user liked using attributes or embeddings; it handles new items but tends to recommend more of the same.
Most sites use implicit feedback such as clicks and purchases, and combine the approaches, often with a ranking model on top.
I'd evaluate offline with ranking metrics like recall at k or NDCG, with time-based splits, and confirm with an online experiment.

key_points.base: Models based on distances (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), penalized models (ridge, lasso) and gradient-based
points: Models based on distances (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), penalized models (ridge, lasso) and gradient-based models like neural networks are sensitive to feature scale: a feature measured in large units dominates distances or gets penalized differently.
Tree-based models split on thresholds, so monotonic rescaling changes nothing.
I fit the scaler on the training data only and apply it to validation and test data, otherwise information leaks.
Standardization is the default; min-max suits bounded inputs but is sensitive to outliers, where a robust scaler helps.
